meta.name: Brew Guide
meta.description: Better coffee at home: one guide per brewing method, with the recipe, timed steps and a table of fixes.
meta.author: Piny

children.text: Brew Guide is better coffee at home. It has one page for each way of brewing: the recipe, the steps with a timer, and what to change when it tastes wrong.
There are six guides: pour-over, AeroPress, French press, moka pot, espresso and cold brew. Every recipe is brewed and tasted by people before it is published, and its test notes say what we changed.
Made by the Pinies in Piny, on EmDash. The photos are from Unsplash.
Every recipe is brewed at home by a person, three times, before it is published. We write down the beans, the grinder and what we changed, and the page says when it was last brewed.

content.text: the method and its weights, for example pour-over, 15 g : 250 g
the roaster and the roast date
how many times, and by whom
published, or back for another try

children.text: A recipe that still tastes wrong after three brews is not published. We change one thing at a time, usually the grind, and start again.
Start here. Every guide on this site depends on three things you control before you brew: the beans, the grind and the water.
Buy whole beans with a roast date on the bag, and use them between one and four weeks after it. Keep them sealed, away from light and heat, and grind just before you brew.
Use water that tastes good on its own; filtered tap water is fine. For hot methods, let a boiled kettle rest for half a minute to reach 90 to 95 °C. Weigh it: 1 ml of water weighs 1 g.
Weigh your coffee. It changes more than any machine.

data.title: Pour-over

$media.alt: Hot water poured over coffee in a pour-over cone

data.excerpt: A clean, bright cup from a cone and a kettle: 15 g of coffee, 250 g of water at 94 °C, done in 3:30.

children.text: Pour-over gives the clearest cup of the six. You pour the water yourself, so the speed of your pour and the size of your grind decide how the coffee tastes. Weigh both, and time the pours.
from the first pour to the last drip
Before you start: put a paper filter in the cone, rinse it with hot water and pour that water away. Add the coffee and shake it flat.
Bloom: pour 40 g of water, enough to wet all the coffee. It puffs up as the gas leaves.
Pour slowly in small circles up to 150 g.
Pour again up to 250 g, keeping the water off the paper.
Give the cone a gentle swirl so the bed settles flat.
The last drips fall. Lift the cone away and serve.

content.text: The water ran through too fast
The water ran through too slowly
Too little coffee for the water
Grind finer, then pour more slowly

children.text: Brewed three times at home by a person. On the first try it ran through in 2:50 and tasted sour, so we ground one step finer and it finished at 3:30.

data.title: AeroPress

$media.alt: Hot water poured into an AeroPress

data.excerpt: A full, sweet cup in two minutes: 15 g of fine coffee, 225 g of water, a stir and a slow press.

children.text: The AeroPress steeps the coffee like a French press and then pushes it through paper, so the cup is full but clean. It is quick, forgiving and easy to wash.
Before you start: put a paper filter in the cap, rinse it and screw the cap on. Stand the AeroPress on a sturdy mug and add the coffee.
Stir three times so all the coffee is wet.
Set the plunger in the top, just enough to hold the coffee in.
Lift the AeroPress and mug together, give them a swirl, and start pressing slowly.
Stop when you hear a hiss. Taste, and add hot water if you like it longer.

content.text: Too short a steep or too coarse a grind
Grind finer, or start pressing at 1:45
Pressed too hard, or too fine a grind
Press gently, grind one step coarser

children.text: Brewed three times at home by a person. We kept the recipe as written; the third cup was the sweetest after a gentler press.

data.title: French press

$media.alt: A French press on a wooden table

data.excerpt: A heavy, rounded cup that needs no paper: 30 g of coarse coffee, 450 g of water, four minutes and a gentle press.

children.text: The French press steeps the coffee in all the water at once and holds back the grounds with a metal mesh. The cup is heavy and rounded, with a little sediment at the bottom.
Before you start: warm the press with hot water and pour it away. Add the coffee.
Pour all 450 g of water and put the lid on, with the plunger up.
Stir the crust on top, and spoon off the foam.
Press the plunger down gently, only to just below the surface, and pour it all out so it stops brewing.

content.text: Grind coarser, and do not press to the bottom
Steep a full 4:00, or use 32 g of coffee
Left in the press too long
Pour every cup out as soon as you press

children.text: Brewed three times at home by a person. Skimming the foam before pressing made the cup cleaner, so it is now a step.

data.title: Moka pot

$media.alt: A moka pot brewing on a stove

data.excerpt: Strong stovetop coffee: water up to the valve, fine coffee left loose, low heat, and off the stove at 5:00.

children.text: The moka pot pushes boiling water up through the coffee with steam. It is not espresso, but it is strong and rich. Low heat, and taking it off at the right moment, make the difference.
hot water up to the valve
Before you start: fill the bottom with just-boiled water up to the valve. Fill the basket with coffee, level it with a finger, and screw the pot together with a towel.
Put the pot on low to medium heat with the lid open.
Coffee starts to rise, dark and slow.
The stream turns pale and starts to sputter.
Take it off the heat and cool the bottom under the cold tap to stop it.

content.text: The heat was too high, or it boiled dry
Lower the heat and stop at the first sputter
Cold water at the start, or too coarse a grind
Start with hot water, grind finer
Brew and throw away two pots, rinse with water only

children.text: Brewed three times at home by a person. Starting with hot water instead of cold took the burnt edge off every cup.

data.title: Espresso

$media.alt: Tamping ground coffee into a portafilter

data.excerpt: A balanced shot: 18 g of coffee in, 36 g of espresso out, in about 28 seconds.

children.text: Espresso is the least forgiving method here. Weigh the coffee in and the espresso out, and time the shot. When it tastes wrong, change one thing at a time: almost always the grind.
, like flour with a little grit
Before you start: let the machine heat fully, about 93 °C at the group. Grind 18 g into a dry basket, level it, and tamp flat and firm.
Lock the handle in, put the cup on the scale and zero it.
Start the pump and the timer together.
The first drops appear, dark and thick.
Stop at 36 g in the cup.

content.text: The shot ran too fast, under 24 s
The shot ran too slow, over 32 s
The water found a channel through the coffee
Break up clumps and tamp level

children.text: Brewed three times at home by a person. The first shot ran in 21 seconds; one step finer brought it to 28.

data.title: Cold brew

$media.alt: Cold brew over ice in a mason jar

data.excerpt: A smooth concentrate for iced coffee: 100 g of coarse coffee in 800 g of cold water for 16 hours.

children.text: Cold brew trades heat for time. The coffee steeps in cold water overnight and gives a smooth, low-acid concentrate that you dilute over ice. It keeps in the fridge for a week.
Put the coffee in a large jar, pour the cold water over it and stir until it is all wet.
Close the jar and put it in the fridge.
Strain through a paper filter or a fine cloth.
To serve: pour one part concentrate and one part water or milk over ice.

content.text: Too short a steep, or too much water
Steep the full 16 h, or dilute less
Steeped too long, or too fine a grind
Strain a second time through paper

children.text: Brewed three times at home by a person. We tried 12, 16 and 20 hours; 16 was the sweetest.

children.text: The first cup finished at 2:50 and tasted sour and thin. That is water running through too fast, so we ground one step finer. The second and third cups finished at 3:30 and tasted sweet and clear, and the recipe was published as it stands.

data.title: Weigh your coffee

$media.alt: Roasted coffee beans in a white bowl

data.excerpt: A scale changes more than any machine. Why every recipe here is written in grams.

children.text: Weigh your coffee. It changes more than any machine.

A scoop of dark beans and a scoop of light beans can differ by a quarter. That is the difference between a weak cup and a strong one, before you change anything else. A kitchen scale that reads in single grams costs less than a bag of good coffee.
Put the brewer on the scale and zero it.
Add the coffee until the scale reads the recipe's number.
Zero again, then pour the water by weight: 1 ml of water weighs 1 g.
Every guide on this site gives its recipe in grams, and every fix assumes you weighed. Start there.

data.title: When it tastes sour, grind one step finer

$media.alt: Tamping ground coffee into a portafilter

data.excerpt: Sour means the water ran through too fast. The grinder is the first thing to change, one step at a time.

children.text: Most cups that taste wrong are sour or bitter. Sour, thin coffee means the water did not take enough from the grounds, usually because it ran through too fast. Bitter, dry coffee means it took too much.

The grind is the strongest dial you have. A finer grind slows the water down and takes more from the coffee; a coarser grind does the opposite. Move it one step, brew again with the same weights, and taste.

content.text: Check your weights and how evenly the water reaches the coffee
